title: An Argmax Principle for Sum-of-Squares Relaxations on the Sphere
authors: Fernando Jeronimo Granha, Pei Wu, Haochen Xu
abstract: We develop an argmax principle for analyzing sum-of-squares relaxations of optimization problems over the unit sphere. Given a feasible pseudo-expectation, we form a polynomial of high-order pseudo-moments, such as $Φ_k(u)=\widetilde{\mathbb E}\langle x,u\rangle^{2k}$. Our guiding principle is that its maximizers are rounding candidates: their local and global optimality conditions reveal the reweighed pseudo-expectation inequalities governing SoS convergence. This viewpoint unifies several problems previously analyzed by rather different techniques.   We obtain three results. First, for Best Separable State, we give a degree-$O(\sqrt{n/ε})$ SoS analysis for approximating $h_{\mathrm{sep}}(P)$ in the perfect-completeness regime, improving and simplifying Barak, Kothari and Steurer (STOC'17). The dependence is essentially tight for inverse-linear gap under the Exponential-Time Hypothesis, matching hardness from $\mathrm{QMA}(2)$ protocols. Second, for the matrix $2\to4$ norm, degree-$O(\sqrt n/ε)$ SoS gives a multiplicative $(1+ε)$ approximation. Barak et al. (STOC'12) previously gave a comparable-time constant-gap decision algorithm; our result gives a multiplicative guarantee and extends to a family of $p\to q$ norms with even $q$. Finally, for degree-$d$ polynomial optimization, we recover the convergence theorem of Bhattiprolu et al. (FOCS'17) with a shorter, more direct proof: degree-$k$ SoS gives approximation ratio $O_d((n/k)^{d/2-1})$.   The paper introduces no new relaxation. Instead, the high-moment argmax gives a common way to read an SoS solution, unifying previously separate convergence analyses and yielding sharper bounds or simpler proofs.
summary: This paper introduces an 'argmax principle' that uses the maximizer of high-moment polynomials to analyze Sum-of-Squares (SoS) relaxations on the unit sphere. It unifies disparate convergence analyses, providing improved bounds for tasks like determining quantum separability and approximating matrix norms. This methodological advance is significant because it offers a common mathematical lens through which multiple complex problems in quantum information can be viewed.
main_problem: Developing a unified 'argmax principle' to analyze Sum-of-Squares (SoS) relaxations for optimization problems defined over the unit sphere.
main_result: The argmax of high-moment pseudo-polynomials provides a common, unifying framework that yields sharper convergence bounds and simpler proofs across various quantum information tasks.
method: The core method involves constructing an auxiliary polynomial based on high-order pseudo-moments ($\Phi_k$) and analyzing its global maximizer to derive necessary conditions for SoS convergence.
model_or_system: The analysis applies to optimization problems over the unit sphere, specifically addressing the Best Separable State (BSS) problem in quantum information theory and approximating various matrix norms ($p 	o q$).
key_observables: Pseudo-expectations ($	ext{eE}$), high-order pseudo-moments ($\Phi_k$), approximation ratios for separability measures, and distance bounds between matrices.
important_parameters: The analysis is sensitive to the gap structure (e.g., inverse-linear gap $\epsilon = \Theta(1/n)$) and the required polynomial degree $k$ relative to system size $n$.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that analyzing the maximizer of the high-moment polynomial is sufficient to characterize the convergence properties of the underlying SoS relaxation.
figures_summary: Not specified in the notes, but the analysis involves bounding distances ($	ext{dist}_F$) between matrices derived from optimization variables $(u, v)$ and a target matrix $W$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the argmax principle by applying it to three distinct problems: BSS (Theorem 1.1), Matrix Norms (Theorem 1.2), and general polynomial optimization convergence (recovering Bhattiprolu et al.'s result). The latter sections detail the rigorous mathematical machinery using Riemannian trust-region methods.
why_interesting: The unification of analysis techniques across quantum separability, norm approximation, and general moment problems via a single principle is highly valuable for theoretical quantum information scientists.
